C-46 (money laundering offences, ss. 462.31 et seq.); Special Economic Measures Act, S.C. 1992, c. 17; United Nations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all general partners, limited partners holding 25% or greater interest, authorized signatories, and beneficial owners against: Global Affairs Canada Consolidated Canadian Autonomous Sanctions List (under SEMA, UN Act, and Magnitsky Act); Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) guidance; UN Security Council consolidated sanctions; and, where US nexus exists, OFAC SDN List and US Treasury guidance. PEP screening must follow FATF Recommendation 12 and FINTRAC guidance on politically exposed persons (domestic and foreign PEPs), including ongoing monitoring, risk-rating of the partnership, and documented escalation to senior management on any positive hit. For this consumer micro-SaaS, standard tier (Low_Risk_Standard) applies; enhanced due diligence is not presumptively required, but continuous sanctions screening is mandatory for each transaction counterparty using Paddle and Lemon Squeezy payment rails.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: BC Corporate Online (British Columbia Corporate Registry, available at corporateonline.gov.bc.ca; name reservation and NUANS name search report are processed through the BC Corporate Registry platform)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Corporate and limited partnership names in British Columbia must be expressed in the English alphabet (Latin script); accents and special characters are generally disallowed except where forming part of a recognized trademark or distinctive identifier; French-language elements are permissible only where linguistically and legally acceptable; the name must include a distinctive element, a descriptive element, and a legal element (e.g., 'Limited Partnership' or 'L.P.') unless exempted; names must not be misleading, suggest government affiliation, or create confusion with existing BC registrants, federal Canadian entities, or registered extra-provincial entities.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon name rejection, the applicant may file a written Request for Name Reconsideration to the Deputy Registrar of Companies (British Columbia Corporate Registry) within 30 days of the refusal, stating the proposed corrected name, the statutory basis under the Limited Partnership Act / Partnership Act, and rebutting the specific claim of confusion or prohibited token usage. The request should be submitted via BC Corporate Online or by email to CorpRegistry@gov.bc.ca. If the reconsideration is denied, the applicant may further appeal to the Minister responsible for the Registry and, failing that, seek judicial review in the Supreme Court of British Columbia. To avoid statutory expiry of the 56-day reservation window, an expedited re-filing (with the applicable name reservation fee) is recommended within 48 hours of a rejection decision.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Virtual office arrangements are acceptable for a consumer micro-SaaS in British Columbia, provided a physical street address in BC, not a post office box, is designated as the registered office; the registered office must be accessible for service of process and official notices during normal business hours; virtual office providers (e.g., registered agent services in Vancouver) are widely recognized by the BC Registry and satisfy commercial substance for the Low_Risk_Standard tier, provided the associated annual filings (Particulars of Limited Partnership, ISC declaration) are maintained.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low (≈10% risk for the first 24 months). The Canada Revenue Agency and the BC Registrar of Companies rarely conduct unannounced on-site inspections for low-risk, non-licensed, IP-only SaaS operations; inspections occur primarily on suspicion of registered-office malfeasance (e.g., returned mail, non-filing of returns, suspicious ISC disclosures) or upon referral from anti-money-laundering enforcement. A fully virtual office in a recognized commercial agent location will not meaningfully increase inspection likelihood.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Limited Partnership Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 265 (as amended), particularly ss. 4-9 (formation and registration) and s. 13 (contributions and limited liability); residual partnership governance under the Partnership Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 348.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registrar of Companies, BC Registries and Mobile Services, Ministry of Finance, Government of British Columbia, Victoria, BC
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Form LP-1 – Declaration for Registration of a Limited Partnership
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital is prescribed for a British Columbia limited partnership. Limited partners must make an actual capital contribution as stated in the partnership records, and no withdrawal may impair the contributed capital or the partnership's obligations. No escrow account or capital deposit is required by the Registrar.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED, as the corporate general partner of the proposed limited partnership, that the Partnership’s capital subscription and admission of all partners set forth in the draft Partnership Agreement are hereby approved and shall take effect upon filing the Declaration. FURTHER RESOLVED, that the registered office of the Partnership in British Columbia and its statutory records repository are established at the address indicated in the Declaration. FURTHER RESOLVED, that [Name] is appointed managing general partner, with authority to operate the Partnership’s cloud software business, and [Name] is appointed secretary responsible for filings and records. FURTHER RESOLVED, that management is authorized to execute and file the Form LP-1 Declaration, pay all registration fees, and engage counsel and accountants to complete the formation.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registries – Corporate Online Name Reservation Service
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a NUANS name search through BC Registries. Request a reservation of the proposed limited partnership name for 56 days. Verify that the name includes a permissible bilingual corporate designation such as 'Limited Partnership', 'L.P.', or the French equivalents, and that it is not confusingly similar to an existing BC corporation, limited partnership, or protected name.
required_dossiers: Completed BC Registries name request form
NUANS name search report
Written authorization from each general partner
Proposed name suffix confirmation
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused or flagged as confusingly similar, choose a revised distinctive name with a new NUANS search or file a written request for reconsideration with the BC Registrar within 30 days, attaching evidence of entitlement to the preferred name.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Drafting and Execution of Partnership Documentation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Legal Counsel / Certified Public Accountant engaged by the partners
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare a limited partnership agreement defining partners, capital contributions, allocation of profits and losses, management authority, and indemnification provisions. Complete Form LP-1 identifying the partnership name, registered office address, full legal names and addresses of all general and limited partners, prescribed place of business in British Columbia, and the contribution limit for the limited partner(s). Obtain original wet-ink or electronic signatures of all general partners as required by the Registrar.
required_dossiers: Draft Limited Partnership Agreement
Form LP-1 – Declaration for Registration
Schedule of Partners and Capital Contributions
Registered office address consent from the owner or service provider
Identification documents for each general partner
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar or filing agent identifies inconsistencies between the declaration and the partnership agreement, cure by executing an amending declaration or amending the partnership agreement, and re-submit for filing before any third-party reliance.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Registration Filing with the Registrar of Companies
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: File the completed Form LP-1 through Corporate Online, or file in person at the BC Registries counter in Victoria, British Columbia. Pay the applicable registration fee (approximately CAD 52 / USD 38). Upon review, the Registrar issues an electronic Certificate of Registration. Confirm the exact legal name, registration number, and registration date on the certificate before executing contracts with third parties.
required_dossiers: Signed Form LP-1 – Declaration for Registration
Payment confirmation for the BC limited partnership registration fee
Corporate Online account authorization or agent authorization form
Copies of notarized identification for non-resident general partners, if applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar issues a deficiency notice or query, the filing agent must respond in writing within 30 days with amended signatures, supplemental affidavits, or corrected declarations. Failure to cure may result in abandonment, but refiling is generally permitted without prejudice.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Establishment of Registered Office and Statutory Records
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registered Office within British Columbia; Registrar of Companies
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Open the registered office at the physical BC address identified in the declaration, and ensure the office is accessible during business hours for service of process. Maintain the statutory records in a secure repository at that address or at the address designated in the declaration, including a register of limited partners, the executed limited partnership agreement, Form LP-1, and the Certificate of Registration. Any later transfer of the registered office must be filed with the Registrar.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Registration
Consent of the registered office provider
Partnership statutory records binder and register of partners
Filing confirmation for the declared registered office address
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar cannot access records or the office is unavailable, immediately file a Notice of Change of Registered Office and restore the records to the new registered office; if served with a compliance inspection notice, file an explanation with the Registrar within 15 days.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Federal and Provincial Tax Registration for the Limited Partnership
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency – Business Registration Online; BC Online / OneStop for provincial accounts
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After obtaining the Certificate of Registration, register the limited partnership for a federal Business Number (BN) through CRA Business Registration Online. In the same process, open any applicable accounts, including GST/HST for taxable supplies, payroll source deductions if employees are hired, and import/export accounts if cross-border software services will be supplied. Register separately with WorkSafeBC and the BC Ministry of Finance for provincial sales tax and employer obligations where applicable. Since the partnership is pass-through, documentation should clearly identify the general partner for administrative compliance.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Registration
Executed Limited Partnership Agreement
Form RC1 – Business Number Registration / CRA online authorization
Legal name and address details of all general partners
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the CRA rejects the BN application due to legal name mismatch or missing information, correct the registry record with the BC Registrar if necessary, then resubmit the RC1 with the corrected Certificate of Registration; in urgent cases, contact the CRA business inquiries line with the file number.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Payment Processor and Merchant Account Readiness
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Financial institutions and payment processors Paddle / Lemon Squeezy
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete merchant onboarding after registration is confirmed. Ensure the trading name entered with Paddle or Lemon Squeezy exactly matches the legal name on the Certificate of Registration to avoid payout and VAT/GST verifiability problems. Prepare a brief due-diligence package covering the business model, SaaS subscription terms, and recurring payment collection compliance if the platform is used as a reseller of record.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Registration
Executed Limited Partnership Agreement
Corporate KYC package for the general partner
Business plan or product description for the Micro-SaaS application
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the payment processor rejects or pauses the merchant account for AML screening, provide a supplementary beneficial-ownership declaration, proof of the immediate general partner, and the Certificate of Registration; request escalation to the merchant underwriting review team with the assigned case number.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: No industrial licensing board is designated for pure software services under ISIC 6201 in British Columbia. If a physical office is opened, the applicable local authority is the municipal business licensing department for that city (e.g., City of Vancouver Business Licensing Office).
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: No provincial industrial operating licence is required for a remote cloud SaaS business; a municipal business licence may be required if the partnership maintains physical office premises in a BC municipality.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Environmental Protection Division, British Columbia Ministry of Environment and Climate Change Strategy
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt – the software operations constitute a non-physical digital service and appear on no EIA screening list under the Environmental Assessment Act. No EIA registration, report, or permit is required.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: No wastewater, VOC or particulate emissions are generated by a pure Micro-SaaS operation. If office premises are leased, comply with municipal sewer bylaws and the BC Recycling Regulation for electronic waste disposal; any emergency cooling equipment or uninterruptible power supply at the office must meet the applicable equipment emission standards under the Environmental Management Act.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Not required for a fully remote cloud software business. If physical office premises are established, obtain a fire safety inspection certificate under the Safety Standards Act, verify the facility’s structural and electrical load capacity, obtain a municipal occupancy permit, and register as an employer with WorkSafeBC for occupational health and safety coverage.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada; online portal: CRA My Business Account and Business Registration Online (BRO). For British Columbia-specific indirect tax, the competent authority is the BC Ministry of Finance, BC Taxpayer Registration, administered separately from the federal GST/HST system.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: For a foreign extra-provincial limited partnership that is not incorporated in Canada, the first step is to obtain a federal 9-digit Business Number (BN) and a GST/HST program account (RP) via CRA Business Registration Online or Form RC1. The foreign LP must provide partnership formation documents, non-resident partner details, authorized representative or agent for service in Canada, and Canadian business address if a permanent establishment exists. Registration for GST/HST is required where the LP makes taxable supplies in Canada and is not a small supplier, or where it is a non-resident supplier of digital services to Canadian recipients under the place-of-supply rules; the general small-supplier threshold is CAD 30,000 of worldwide taxable supplies in the current or immediately preceding four calendar quarters. If Paddle or Lemon Squeezy acts as merchant of record, the platform may be the registrant responsible for Canadian GST/HST, and the LP should confirm contractual responsibility before direct registration. For BC PST, a separate registration at BC Taxpayer Registration is required if the LP makes taxable sales or leases of taxable software or other PST-liable supplies in BC.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada does not have a check-the-box classification regime. A BC limited partnership is fiscally transparent for Canadian income tax purposes: under Income Tax Act section 96, partnership income is computed at the partnership level but allocated to partners, and each partner is assessed on their allocable share. For foreign partners, Canadian tax exposure depends on whether the LP carries on business in Canada through a permanent establishment; the partnership is not an entity-level taxpayer. For U.S. federal tax purposes, a Canadian limited partnership may file IRS Form 8832 to elect entity classification if the Canadian entity is an eligible entity, or may be treated by default as a partnership if it has more than one member. Hybrid mismatch implications must be reviewed under Income Tax Act sections 18.4 and 18.5 and the OECD BEPS Action 2 framework where the Canadian LP is held through a U.S. partnership or corporation.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) / Harmonized Sales Tax (HST) and British Columbia Provincial Sales Tax (PST). The federal GST rate is 5%; BC applies separate PST at 7% to taxable software and other taxable supplies, giving a combined potential rate of 12% where both taxes apply.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 gross worldwide taxable supplies in a single calendar quarter or in the immediately preceding four consecutive calendar quarters (small-supplier threshold). Non-resident suppliers of digital services to Canadian consumers should assess CRA place-of-supply rules; a non-resident making taxable supplies in Canada in the course of carrying on business in Canada must register regardless of the threshold if the supply is made in Canada, and merchant-of-record platforms may trigger a separate registration obligation under the Excise Tax Act.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada has no mandatory national real-time fiscal clearance, continuous transaction controls, or digital stamping requirement for GST/HST invoices. CRA accepts electronic invoices provided they are accurate, complete, legible, and readily accessible. GST/HST returns must be filed electronically through GST/HST NETFILE or an approved certified software supplier when registration is active. BC does not currently impose a separate real-time electronic invoice clearance mandate for PST.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Under section 23 of the Excise Tax Act and Part V of Schedule VI, exported goods are generally zero-rated. Services supplied to a non-resident recipient may be zero-rated where the service is acquired for consumption or use exclusively outside Canada and is supplied to a non-resident; for lightly regulated cloud-based SaaS subscription services, a supply made over the internet to a foreign consumer is generally zero-rated when the ordinary residence of the recipient is outside Canada and the supply is not delivered to a Canadian address. The supplier must retain contemporaneous evidence of non-resident status, foreign delivery, and payment from abroad.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Canada Border Services Agency export declaration (eManifest/B13-Customs Coding Form) — required for physical goods exports; not required for pure digital SaaS exports
Bill of Lading or airway waybill — physical goods only; for digital SaaS, equivalent evidence includes service delivery logs and IP/geo-location metadata
Inward Remittance Certificate or foreign exchange/bank advice showing receipt of foreign-sourced consideration within the repatriation period — best-practice audit evidence
Subscription agreements and merchant-of-record platform reports from Paddle or Lemon Squeezy demonstrating the recipient's non-resident status and delivery of digital services outside Canada
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA may deny zero-rating and reassess uncollected GST/HST where the supplier cannot substantiate the non-resident status and foreign use of the service. Penalties include the false-statement penalty of 25% of any excess refund or rebate claimed, wilful evasion penalties of up to 50% of tax evaded plus interest, and potential director or partner liability. GAAR and general anti-avoidance reassessments may also apply where GST/HST registrants restructure digital sales to obtain a zero-rating benefit without genuine foreign supply.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) in conjunction with the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) and the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC). Canada operates a liberalised foreign exchange regime; the Minister of Finance and the Bank of Canada jointly manage the exchange rate framework, but the Bank of Canada exercises no discretionary exchange-control licensing powers.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is fully convertible for both current and capital account transactions. There are no exchange-control laws, no restrictions on the repatriation of capital, and no approval mechanism comparable to the International Monetary Fund Article VIII exchange-restriction regime. Dividends, interest, royalties, and partnership distributions may be remitted to non-resident partners and shareholders without foreign-exchange approval, subject solely to income tax withholding pursuant to Part XIII of the Income Tax Act (Canada), treaty reductions, and tax-compliance filings. For a British Columbia limited partnership, the conversion premise is that CAD-denominated liquidity may be converted to any major currency through authorised financial institutions at market rates without regulatory pre-clearance. The practical legal hurdles are documentary: banks require a valid partnership registration, beneficial ownership declarations, tax residency self-certification, and anti-money-laundering screening before permitting outward wires, but there is no sovereign exchange-ticket or surrender requirement.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada does not impose any statutory requirement to surrender export proceeds to a central bank, to maintain export retention accounts, or to convert a mandatory proportion of export revenues into Canadian currency. A BC limited partnership may retain export proceeds in any eligible foreign-currency account, convert such proceeds at negotiated commercial rates, and deploy those funds for working capital, distributions to partners, or reinvestment. For non-resident partners, the only statutory constraints arise from tax law (e.g. withholding under Part XIII and section 212 of the Income Tax Act) and from bank-level documentation of source of funds, not from currency-exchange surrender rules. Trade settlement documentation for software subscriptions does not require a special export declaration as there is no physical movement of goods; the exporter must simply maintain accurate accounting records and issue GST/HST-compliant invoices where applicable.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Royal Bank of Canada (RBC Royal Bank)
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational Account (CAD and USD multi-currency operating envelope)

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Toronto-Dominion Bank Canada Trust (TD Canada Trust)
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational Account and ancillary USD clearing account

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Bank of Montreal (BMO Bank of Montreal)
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Capital Escrow Account or Partner Funded Trust Account, with treasury management overlay
Operational Account with integrated commercial foreign-exchange dealing desk
Operational Account and cross-border USD clearing rail for SaaS merchant payouts

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Low-to-Medium. Foreign electronic money institutions (EMIs) and pure digital non-bank payment providers are not recognised as 'banks' in Canada and may not accept deposits in the deeply regulated sense under the Bank Act (Canada). A non-resident EMI may lawfully assist a BC limited partnership in payment processing if the EMI is regulated in its home jurisdiction and if it does not create a 'deposit-taking' nexus triggering the Bank Act or so-called 'business of moneys lent' restrictions. The safer structure is to use a Canadian-registered MSB (money services business) that is registered with FINTRAC, or a card-payment aggregator (Paddle/Lemon Squeezy as merchant of record), rather than attempting to rely on an offshore EMI for primary treasury clearing. Legal constraints also include the Canadian prohibition on making unauthorised payment services available to Canadian clients without FINTRAC registration where the service constitutes an MSB activity, plus the provincial corporate registration threshold in British Columbia under the Partnership Act if the EMI were to take partnership-facing treasury operations. Viability tier is therefore 'Low' for full primary-banking replacement, but 'Medium' as a supplementary payout corridor for cross-border software subscription receipts.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: There is no statutory Canadian rule requiring that partners, directors, or general partners of a BC limited partnership physically appear at a bank branch to open a corporate account. Remote account opening is permitted under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act and associated regulations, provided that the financial institution verifies identity using a prescribed method such as dual-sided government-issued ID scanning, credible-person attestation, or use of a Canadian digital identity verification service. However, risk-based compliance policies at major Canadian banks typically impose stronger due diligence for non-resident or ’foreign-controlling’ limited partnerships: the general partner (or its authorised signatory) must produce notarised identification and, in many cases, complete a video or in-person interview with a branch compliance officer. The ’mandate’ is therefore effectively institution-specific: no physical appearance is legally mandated, but banks may treat physical presence as a de facto condition for granting treasury overrides, high wire limits, or FX trading lines to a newly formed partnership without domestic directors. For firms using Paddle/Lemon Squeezy, the underlying merchant funds are remitted to the LP’s CAD clearing account; the bank will still require the LP to satisfy KYC by establishing who is the ultimate beneficial owner, the source of funds, and the purpose of the international flows.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Entity opacity and inability of the bank to identify the natural-person beneficial owners of the BC limited partnership, particularly where the general partner is itself a corporate trustee or a hybrid entity.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide a current Certificate of Limited Partnership issued by the BC Corporate Online registry; a certified copy of the Limited Partnership Agreement; a certified extract of the BC Register of Partners and general partner records; a written beneficial ownership schedule identifying each person owning 25% or more of the partnership and each person exercising direct or indirect control; personal identification for those persons; and an up-to-date provincial search confirming no dissolution, suspension, or amalgamation condition.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident/multi-jurisdictional tax residency mismatch raising Fatca, Common Reporting Standard, or Canada Revenue Agency reporting flags, especially if the LP is treated as a pass-through entity but partners reside in treaty jurisdictions.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Submit a Canada Revenue Agency Form NR403 or equivalent partnership non-resident declaration where applicable; signed Canada-US or relevant treaty residency self-certification forms (IRS Form W-8BEN-E for look-through partnership, or Canadian Form RC518/RC519 equivalent); the partnership’s most recent CRA confirmation of registration for a business number; and a written tax transparency memorandum that maps each partner’s jurisdiction of tax residence and the applicable withholding position under the Canada–US treaty or the relevant comprehensive income tax treaty.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Source-of-wealth and source-of-funds opacity circling around internet-origin subscription revenue, consumer chargebacks, and merchant-aggregator settlement flows from Paddle or Lemon Squeezy.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Deliver clean bank statements of the merchant aggregator payouts for 12 months; executed Merchant of Record agreements with Paddle or Lemon Squeezy; a statement of charges, refunds, chargebacks, and fees; a description of the SaaS dashboard and subscriber lifecycle; corroborating invoices to end customers; and management representations regarding customer locations and geographical sales tax or GST/HST treatment.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Sanctions/Proliferation-financing exposure, including any suspicion that end-users or distributors may include sanctioned persons in Crimea, Russia, Syria, Iran, North Korea, or other restricted locations.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide an automated or manual sanctions screening policy; geolocation and IP-address-based blocklist architecture used by the SaaS platform; a written representation that no partners, customers, or principals are located in or are owned/controlled by sanctioned jurisdictions; supporting malware/clean IP logs from the payment processor; and a compliance attestation executed by the general partner confirming prohibition of US SDN-list or Canada's Consolidated Canadian Autonomous Sanctions List exposure.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Transactional footprint mismatch for a ’micro-SaaS’ profile: repeated small inbound transfers from merchant aggregators mixed with fast outbound conduit distributions may resemble layering or round-tripping.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Prepare a treasury flow diagram; reconcile bank statements against merchant settlement reports; provide a profit-distribution policy and minutes of the general partner approving distributions; provide invoices or contracts for subcontractor and software vendor payments; and offer access to an independent bookkeeping ledger demonstrating that every CAD outflow is matched to an operating expense or a capital transaction.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound equity subscriptions and capital contributions to a BC limited partnership from non-resident partners are routed through the SWIFT MT103 message type for cross-border wire transfers. The wire must include the receiving bank’s institution number, branch/transit number, and the LP’s bank account number; the beneficiary line should read the exact legal name of the partnership as registered in British Columbia. For purpose codes, Canadian banks do not use the US Federal Reserve BOP code regime, but remittance information should state either ’Capital contribution to limited partnership’ or ’Trust/escrow deposit for partnership equity subscription’ in forwarding instructions. The bank will require proof of source of funds, typically in the form of a partner guarantee, signed capital subscription, funds-origin affidavit, and a notarised copy of the partnership agreement. Where the capital is raised through an intermediate Luxembourg/Hong-Kong entity, clear a mirror SWIFT record and show the ultimate partner on the SWIFT field 50K to avoid AML routing flags. On receipt, the LP’s bank balance will be held as CAD or, if open, as a foreign-currency account; if the capital is USD-denominated, the bank will quote a spot conversion to CAD or will keep the USD as a separate no-repatriation currency position depending on the account class. No Bank of Canada foreign-exchange approval is needed.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: For trade settlements and operating disbursements, the preferred clearing rails are (i) SWIFT MT103 for cross-border vendor payments and partner distributions, (ii) LVTS (Large Value Transfer System) or the real-time RTR (Real-Time Rail, where commercially available) for CAD-denominated payments to domestic vendors, and (iii) a Commercial Letter of Credit (typically documentary credit under UCP600) for any physical-equipment purchase or software-development outsourcing that requires payment against delivery of deliverables. Because the target business is a consumer micro-SaaS receiving payments through Paddle or Lemon Squeezy, the principal outbound movement is the monthly/quarterly settlement sweep from the merchant-of-record into the LP’s operating account, followed by tax payments to the CRA, subscriptions to cloud infrastructure, and distributions to partners. These recurring outflows should be executed using automated clearing house (ACH) in Canada for domestic gives, and SWIFT MT103 for cross-border. If the LP imports licensed software or acquires an overseas codebase, a usance Letter of Credit or SWIFT-based document collection may be used, but the prudent default for a pass-through LP is to avoid trade instruments and instead use clean wire settlements under a standard master services agreement.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Outright FX forwards between CAD and USD, GBP, EUR through a commercial bank under an International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) 2002 Master Agreement or Canadian Master Agreement for Short-Term Foreign Exchange Transactions
Participating forwards and flexible forwards offered by Canadian Schedule I banks as risk-management products for committed trade flows

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) are not genuinely needed for CAD because the currency is fully convertible; however, certain Canadian banks may offer an NDF-equivalent structure if the partnership uses a closed offshore pricing model, subject to bank policy and derivatives qualification
Cross-currency swaps for partnership capital base management, available only when both counterparties satisfy ISDA and Credit Support Annex collateral requirements
Vanilla over-the-counter (OTC) call or put options on CAD/USD executed through the bank’s FX desk, used to cap distribution-repatriation conversion costs without speculative leverage

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: BC Limited Partnership Annual Report (Yearly Report) — online filing through BC Registry (Form AR/LP)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: BC Corporate Registry — Registrar of Companies, Ministry of Finance, Province of British Columbia
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annually by the last day of the month following the month of the LP's registration anniversary (e.g., an LP registered in March files by April 30 each year), beginning with the reporting year after registration.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to file the yearly report for two consecutive years exposes the LP to administrative dissolution and strike-off by the Registrar after notice; a dissolved LP loses legal capacity to carry on business in BC. Restoration requires payment of all outstanding annual-report fees plus a registrar restoration fee of approximately USD 150–220 (C$200–300); persons knowingly permitting continued default are liable to offence fines under the Limited Partnership Act.

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: Federal 15% + British Columbia 12% = 27% combined general corporate rate; eligible CCPC active business income taxed at 9% federal + 2% BC = 11% (Small Business Deduction on first CAD 500,000). The LP itself is fiscally transparent; partners pay tax on allocated income.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) Small Business Deduction (SBD) reducing combined rate to 11% on first CAD 500,000 of active business income; Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) investment tax credits (ITCs) up to 35% on qualifying R&D expenditures; 100% capital cost allowance (CAA) on eligible computer hardware/software under Class 12/52 (accelerated CCA); Patent Box-style Income Deduction proposed (use of patent/CIS principal treatment).
